title: Unreal Present Conditions and Wishes
summary: Describe a present situation that is different from reality, explain its imagined result, and express wishes about current facts, abilities or obligations. Use past forms for unreal meaning without confusing them with events in the past.
learningObjectives: Express a situation contrary to present facts with if + past simple and would + base verb.
Use wish + past simple to say a current situation is not as desired.
Express a wished-for ability with wish + could and a wished-for absence of obligation with wish + did not have to.
Use were or was appropriately after hypothetical if and wish, and avoid would in ordinary unreal if-clauses.

explanation.heading: Past grammar, present meaning
explanation.body: For an imaginary or unreal situation now, the if-clause uses a past form, even though the meaning is about the present. The main clause usually uses would + base verb to give an imagined result. Contrast this with a normal past-tense story: a hypothetical past form does not mean the imagined event actually took place.
explanation.example: If my flat had thicker walls, I would hear less street noise.

explanation.heading: Wish + past for an unsatisfactory present fact
explanation.body: Use I wish + subject + past form when reality is different from what you want now. The wish itself does not change the fact. After wish, did not, had, knew, were and other past forms commonly describe present regrets. Do not use I wish + would simply to replace these past forms when expressing your own present situation.
explanation.example: I wish my local library stayed open later on weekdays.

explanation.heading: Wishing for abilities and freedom from obligations
explanation.body: Wish + could + base verb expresses an ability or possibility that is missing now. Wish + did not have to + base verb expresses regret about an existing obligation. In imagined if-clauses, could can describe an ability the person does not currently possess; in a result clause, could often means would be able to.
explanation.example: I wish I could understand the announcements at the station.

explanation.heading: Was and were in unreal situations
explanation.body: After hypothetical if and wish, were is possible with all subjects and is particularly common in careful or formal English. Was also occurs with I, he, she and it in everyday speech. If I were you is a fixed and widely preferred advice pattern. Whichever form you use, make the main clause consistent with an imagined situation.
explanation.example: If I were in charge of the café, I would add more vegetarian meals.

explanation.heading: Keep would out of ordinary unreal conditions
explanation.body: In the usual unreal-present pattern, put the past form in the if-clause and would in the imagined result: if I lived, I would walk. Similarly, use wish + past for a present fact: I wish I knew, not I wish I would know. A separate use of wish + would for desired changes or behavior belongs to a different lesson.
explanation.example: If we lived on the ground floor, moving furniture would be easier.

left.label: Reality now
left.example: Our kitchen has no natural light.
left.note: This states an actual present limitation.

right.label: Unreal result
right.example: If our kitchen had a window, it would be brighter.
right.note: Had marks a different present situation; would marks the imagined effect.

comparisons.title: Wish for a fact versus wish for an ability

left.label: Present fact
left.example: I wish the bus stop were closer.
left.note: Wish + past describes a present fact I would like to change.

right.label: Missing ability
right.example: I wish I could read music.
right.note: Wish + could expresses an ability I do not have at present.

left.label: Were
left.example: I wish the office were less noisy.
left.note: Were is standard for hypothetical meaning, especially in more careful language.

right.label: Was
right.example: I wish the office was less noisy.
right.note: Was is also heard and accepted in everyday English with a singular subject.

examples.sentence: If my schedule were more flexible, I would visit my family more often.
examples.note: Were describes an imagined present arrangement; would visit describes its result.

examples.sentence: I wish I did not have to work this Sunday.
examples.note: Did not have to describes an unwanted obligation that still exists.

examples.sentence: If Hana could draw, she could help with the posters.
examples.note: The first could means she had the ability; the second means she would be able to help.

examples.sentence: I wish the footpath were wider here.
examples.note: The speaker would prefer a different situation now; the path is currently narrow.

examples.sentence: I would buy fewer takeaway meals if I knew how to cook more dishes.
examples.note: The result precedes the if-clause; the hypothetical meaning is unchanged.

examples.sentence: If I were you, I would ask for a quieter table.
examples.note: If I were you offers advice from an imagined position.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I wish I know the answer.
commonMistakes.correct: I wish I knew the answer.
commonMistakes.why: A regret about not knowing something now uses a past form after wish.

commonMistakes.incorrect: If I would have a garden, I would grow herbs.
commonMistakes.correct: If I had a garden, I would grow herbs.
commonMistakes.why: Use the past simple in an ordinary hypothetical if-clause, not would + base verb.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I wish I can read the sign from here.
commonMistakes.correct: I wish I could read the sign from here.
commonMistakes.why: Wish + could expresses a present ability that is missing.

commonMistakes.incorrect: If I were taller, I will reach the top shelf.
commonMistakes.correct: If I were taller, I would reach the top shelf.
commonMistakes.why: Use would in the hypothetical result instead of will.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I wish I do not have to work late today.
commonMistakes.correct: I wish I did not have to work late today.
commonMistakes.why: Use past-form did not have to after wish to regret a present obligation.

studyTips: Write the real fact in the margin before each hypothetical: I live far away → If I lived closer, I would walk.
Practise the two meanings of could by putting it once inside the if-clause (ability) and once in the result (opportunity).
Convert a present complaint into a precise wish; check that the verb after wish moves back into a past form without changing the time meaning.

exercises.prompt: You cannot see the sea from your apartment. Choose the unreal present condition: “If our building ___ taller, we would have a sea view.”
exercises.feedback: Were expresses a present situation different from the real one; would belongs in the result.

exercises.prompt: You must attend a long meeting tomorrow and regret that obligation: “I wish I ___ attend the meeting.”
exercises.feedback: Wish + didn’t have to can express regret about an obligation that is still scheduled.

exercises.prompt: You have not learned to ride a bicycle. “I wish I ___ ride one.”
exercises.feedback: Could after wish describes a desired ability the speaker lacks.

exercises.prompt: Your friend wants advice about a difficult conversation. “If I ___ you, I would talk to her privately.”
exercises.feedback: If I were you is a standard way to introduce advice about an unreal position.

exercises.prompt: You do not own a car. Use the past form of have for an unreal condition: “If I ___ a car, I would drive to the coast.”
acceptedAnswers: had
exercises.feedback: Had expresses imaginary present possession, not a past event.

exercises.prompt: The office is noisy now. Use the hypothetical form of be (accept either standard form): “I wish the office ___ quieter.”
acceptedAnswers: were
was
exercises.feedback: Were is often preferred for unreal wishes; was is also possible with a singular subject.

exercises.prompt: You are required to wear a uniform and dislike this. Complete the phrase with the negative past form of have to: “I wish I ___ wear a uniform.”
acceptedAnswers: didn't have to
did not have to
exercises.feedback: The speaker wishes a present obligation did not exist; use did not have to.

exercises.prompt: You are unable to speak Italian now. Express the missing ability with a modal: “If I ___ speak Italian, I would apply for that role.”
acceptedAnswers: could
exercises.feedback: Could expresses the unreal ability needed to apply.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I wish I would know the answer to this question.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I knew the answer to this question.
exercises.feedback: For a regret about missing knowledge now, use wish + knew, not wish + would know.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: If I would live near the station, I could take an earlier train.
acceptedAnswers: If I lived near the station, I could take an earlier train.
exercises.feedback: An ordinary hypothetical if-clause uses past simple lived; could in the result expresses opportunity.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I wish I can understand the guide without subtitles.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I could understand the guide without subtitles.
exercises.feedback: Replace can with could after wish to describe an ability you do not have.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: If I were the manager, I will allow flexible hours.
acceptedAnswers: If I were the manager, I would allow flexible hours.
If I were the manager, I'd allow flexible hours.
exercises.feedback: Use would, not will, to describe the result of an unreal present condition.

speakingExercises.prompt: You currently live too far from the office to walk there. Imagine living nearby. Make one sentence beginning “If I lived near the office” and ending “to work”. Use would + walk.
acceptedAnswers: If I lived near the office, I would walk to work.
If I lived near the office, I'd walk to work.
speakingExercises.feedback: Lived is a hypothetical past form for a present situation; would walk is the imagined result.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your balcony overlooks a noisy avenue. Express a wish for less traffic noise. Begin “I wish the avenue” and use the adjective quieter.
acceptedAnswers: I wish the avenue were quieter.
I wish the avenue was quieter.
speakingExercises.feedback: Were or was after wish introduces a different present situation.

speakingExercises.prompt: You cannot swim, and you regret that. Give a short complete sentence beginning “I wish”. Use could.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I could swim.
speakingExercises.feedback: Wish + could describes the ability to swim, which is missing now.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend keeps working late and feels exhausted. Give the advice to leave work earlier, starting “If I were you”. Use would.
acceptedAnswers: If I were you, I would leave work earlier.
If I were you, I'd leave work earlier.
speakingExercises.feedback: If I were you introduces an imagined viewpoint; would gives the advice.

speakingExercises.prompt: You cannot grow vegetables because your home has no outdoor space. Express an unreal condition about having a garden, followed by “we could grow vegetables”. Begin “If we”.
acceptedAnswers: If we had a garden, we could grow vegetables.
speakingExercises.feedback: Had introduces unreal present possession; could grow expresses the resulting opportunity.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct just the verb after wish and say the full sentence: “I wish my phone is easier to use.”
acceptedAnswers: I wish my phone were easier to use.
I wish my phone was easier to use.
speakingExercises.feedback: Wish about a present fact takes a past form: were or was.

speakingExercises.prompt: You have to work on Saturdays, but you want that obligation to disappear. Begin “I wish” and use the expression “have to work on Saturdays” in the appropriate negative past form.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I didn't have to work on Saturdays.
I wish I did not have to work on Saturdays.
speakingExercises.feedback: Wish + did not have to expresses regret about a present obligation.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your apartment has no spare room, so you cannot invite your cousin to stay. Say two sentences: first an “I wish” sentence about having a spare room; then an “If I had” sentence about inviting your cousin. Repeat “a spare room” in both.
acceptedAnswers: I wish I had a spare room. If I had a spare room, I would invite my cousin.
I wish I had a spare room. If I had a spare room, I'd invite my cousin.
speakingExercises.feedback: Wish describes a present regret; if + past and would describe an imagined consequence.

listeningExercises.prompt: What present problem does the speaker want to change?
choices: The office has too many meeting rooms
There is no separate quiet room for calls
listeningExercises.feedback: The wish identifies a missing quiet room; currently calls happen at desks.
listeningExercises.audioText: I wish our office had a quiet room. At the moment everyone takes calls at their desks.

listeningExercises.prompt: Why can the speaker not give reliable directions?
choices: They do not know the area
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker would help if they knew the route, but they lack that knowledge.
listeningExercises.audioText: If I knew the way to the sports centre, I would guide you, but I've never been to that neighbourhood.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the negative obligation phrase heard between “I wish I” and “catch”.
acceptedAnswers: didn't have to
did not have to
listeningExercises.feedback: Didn’t have to expresses regret about a current obligation.
listeningExercises.audioText: I wish I didn't have to catch the first train every morning.

listeningExercises.prompt: What would change if the imagined condition became real?
choices: The room would have fewer windows
The room would receive more natural light
listeningExercises.feedback: Larger windows would allow more daylight into the living room.
listeningExercises.audioText: If the windows in our living room were larger, we would get more daylight. Right now they are tiny.

listeningExercises.prompt: Why is the speaker unwilling to lend the headphones?
choices: Theo has never asked to borrow them
The speaker has already sold them
Theo previously damaged the speaker’s belongings
listeningExercises.feedback: The unreal if-clause identifies a lack of trust based on earlier damage.
listeningExercises.audioText: I'd lend Theo my headphones if I trusted him with them, but he damaged my last pair.

listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker want to be able to do?
listeningExercises.feedback: Wish + could shows that the speaker lacks the required cycling ability at present.
listeningExercises.audioText: I wish I could join the long cycling tour, but I can't ride that far yet.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word hypothetical verb phrase immediately before “those articles”.
acceptedAnswers: would read
listeningExercises.feedback: Would read states the imagined result of being fluent.
listeningExercises.audioText: If I were fluent in Korean, I would read those articles without translation.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the negative past form directly between “upstairs” and “so loud”.
acceptedAnswers: weren't
were not
listeningExercises.feedback: Weren’t follows wish to express an unsatisfactory present situation.
listeningExercises.audioText: I wish the neighbours upstairs weren't so loud late at night.
